scope.excluded: Couples living together but not married or in a civil partnership. Anyone already claiming Married Couple's Allowance. A higher earner above the basic rate — above £50,270, or above £43,662 for a Scottish taxpayer.

scope.excluded: Anyone whose trading income comes from a company they control, a partnership they are in, or their own or their partner's employer. It cannot be combined with claiming actual expenses — it is one or the other.

title: Council Tax Reduction

scope.excluded: People subject to immigration control, and people not habitually resident in the UK, Ireland, the Channel Islands or the Isle of Man, are excluded by law from every council's scheme. scope.excluded: Anyone who meets none of the criteria and has had no notice to file. No payments on account are due where last year's bill was under £1,000, or where more than 80% of last year's tax was already collected at source. The paper deadline was 31 October 2026 and has passed.
scope.from_when: For the 2025/26 tax year
scope.how_to_claim: File online and pay by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027.

notes: THREE obligations fall on 31 January 2027, not one: the return, the balancing payment for 2025/26, and the first payment on account for 2026/27. Payments on account include Class 4 National Insurance but not Capital Gains Tax or student loan repayments. Budget 2026 changed nothing here; more frequent in-year payments start only from April 2029.

title: VAT registration and deregistration thresholds

figures.what: Registration threshold — taxable turnover in any rolling 12 months
The forward-look test, which triggers immediate registration
Deregistration threshold — you may ask HMRC to cancel below this
Time to register after the end of the month you went over

scope.excluded: Businesses selling only goods or services that are VAT exempt or outside the scope of VAT, whatever their turnover. Businesses at £90,000 or below, who may still register voluntarily. Businesses whose supplies are wholly or mainly zero-rated can apply for exemption from registration.
scope.from_when: Unchanged since 1 April 2024, and confirmed unchanged for April 2026 and April 2027 at Budget 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Register online with HMRC within 30 days of the end of the month the test was breached.

notes: ROLLING 12 months — any consecutive twelve, checked monthly. NOT the tax year, NOT the accounting year, NOT profit. Turnover is sales value before costs. Zero-rated sales count; exempt and out-of-scope sales do not. The forward-look test is the next 30 DAYS, so one large contract can trigger it.

title: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

figures.what: Qualifying income in 2024/25 — in scope since 6 April 2026
Qualifying income in 2025/26 — in scope from 6 April 2027
Qualifying income in 2026/27 — in scope from 6 April 2028

scope.who: Sole traders and landlords in Self Assessment whose qualifying income — gross self-employment and property income added together, before expenses — exceeds the threshold for the year
scope.excluded: Anyone with qualifying income of £20,000 or less is automatically exempt with nothing to apply for. Partnerships are not in yet. Employees and company directors with no self-employment or property income are outside it entirely, and limited company profits stay under Corporation Tax. Various further exemptions exist, including for foster and kinship carers.
scope.from_when: Live since 6 April 2026 for the first tranche
scope.how_to_claim: Sign up through HMRC's service and use compatible software for quarterly updates and a final declaration.

notes: Qualifying income is GROSS, not profit, and the two sources are added together. The look-back is two years, so the 6 April 2027 start is set by the 2025/26 return being filed now. Being exempt does NOT remove the duty to file an ordinary Self Assessment return. Budget 2026 added a penalty easement for the April 2027 cohort and new exemptions, but did not move the thresholds.

title: CIS monthly returns

Deduction for a subcontractor registered for CIS
Deduction where the subcontractor is not registered, or HMRC cannot match their details
Penalties at 1 day, 2 months, and 6 and 12 months late

scope.who: Every CIS contractor — construction businesses paying subcontractors, and businesses outside construction spending over £3 million on construction in the previous 12 months
scope.excluded: Householders having work done on their own home are not contractors and file nothing. Subcontractors do not file these returns at all — the duty is the contractor's. A contractor who has notified HMRC of a period of inactivity, up to 6 months.

scope.how_to_claim: File the CIS300 online by the 19th. With no payments made, file a nil return or notify inactivity by the same date.

notes: The 19th is a RECEIPT deadline and does not move for weekends or bank holidays. Penalties stack. The 30% rate also applies when HMRC simply cannot match the subcontractor's details. Deductions come from the LABOUR element only — materials and VAT are excluded. Budget 2026 contained no CIS measure.

title: Companies House confirmation statement

figures.what: How often a confirmation statement must be filed
Filing window after the end of the review period
The fee
Fine for failing to file, and the company may be struck off

scope.who: Every company on the register, including dormant and non-trading companies
scope.excluded: Sole traders, ordinary partnerships and unincorporated bodies file nothing, because they are not registered companies. A company already dissolved and removed from the register. No fee is due on a second statement filed within the same 12-month payment period.
scope.from_when: First review period ends 12 months after incorporation
scope.how_to_claim: File online within 14 days of the end of the review period, or by paper form CS01.

notes: NOT the annual accounts and NOT the Corporation Tax return — a separate, third filing, and a company that files accounts on time can still be struck off for missing this. There is no 'nothing to report' exemption: the duty is to CONFIRM. Failure is a criminal offence and directors can be prosecuted. Companies House fees are set administratively, not by the Budget.

title: Payments on Account

figures.value: 2 payments a year, due by midnight on 31 January and 31 July
figures.what: the payment-on-account deadlines; the instalment due 31 January 2027 is the first payment on account for 2026/27, paid alongside the 2025/26 balancing payment

each payment on account is usually half of the tax you owed the previous year; HMRC manual: 50% of the 'relevant amount' for the preceding year, being income tax assessed less tax deducted at source (s.59A(2) TMA 1970)
de minimis: no payments on account are due if the amount of tax you owed last year was less than £1,000 (HMRC manual: 'less than a fixed amount of £1,000')

deducted-at-source test: no payments on account are due if last year you paid more than 80% of the tax you owed outside Self Assessment (HMRC manual: the relevant amount bears a proportion to the assessed amount of less than 1 to 5)
deadline for the balancing payment, worked out by deducting the payments on account already made from the total tax owed
how to claim to reduce payments on account if you expect your tax to be lower than last year

scope.who: Self Assessment taxpayers whose last year's Self Assessment tax bill was £1,000 or more and who paid 20% or more of that tax through Self Assessment rather than at source. The payment due by midnight on 31 January 2027 is the first payment on account towards 2026/27, calculated as half of the 2025/26 'relevant amount' (income tax assessed less tax deducted at source), and falls due at the same time as the 2025/26 balancing payment.
scope.excluded: No payments on account are due if EITHER the amount of tax owed for the previous year was less than £1,000, OR more than 80% of the tax owed for the previous year was paid outside Self Assessment (e.g. through a PAYE tax code or tax already deducted by a bank). Per HMRC manual SALF303 the statutory tests are the £1,000 fixed de minimis and the 'less than 1 to 5' proportion test under s.59A(1) TMA 1970. Payments on account also do not cover Capital Gains Tax or Class 2 National Insurance, which are collected in the balancing payment.
scope.from_when: Standing rule under s.59A Taxes Management Act 1970; the next instalment is due by midnight on 31 January 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — HMRC calculates the instalments from your previous year's return and they are due without demand. To REDUCE them, sign in to your online account, select the option to view your latest Self Assessment return and select 'Reduce payments on account', or send form SA303 to your tax office, stating the amount you expect to owe. If you reduce them and your actual bill turns out higher, HMRC charges interest on the difference.

notes: Verified against both the gov.uk guidance page and HMRC manual SALF303 (which cites s.59A TMA 1970 and the limits originally set by SI 1996/1654 as amended). Both the £1,000 and 80% tests are alternatives — either one removes the obligation. SALF303 confirms payments are 'due without demand'.

title: Self Assessment Late Filing Penalties

figures.what: initial fixed late filing penalty, charged as soon as the return is late, regardless of whether any tax is owed

figures.value: £10 per day, up to a maximum of £900
figures.what: daily penalties once the return is more than 3 months late (HMRC manual: £10 a day over a period of 90 days); HMRC must decide that a daily penalty is payable and give notice to the taxpayer

figures.value: 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater
figures.what: further penalty after 6 months (HMRC manual: the greater of 5% of the tax liability which would have been shown in the return, and £300)

figures.value: 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater
figures.what: further penalty after 12 months; can rise to 70% of the tax due where information is deliberately withheld, and 100% where that withholding is concealed

the replacement penalty for taxpayers inside Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — a points-based system where each missed return deadline earns one point and a £200 penalty is charged at 4 points, and for each further missed deadline

scope.who: Anyone required to file a Self Assessment tax return who misses the filing deadline. For the 2025/26 return the online filing deadline is 31 January 2027. The penalties stack: £100 immediately, then £10 a day from 3 months late (max £900), then the greater of 5% of the tax due or £300 at 6 months, and the same again at 12 months. All partners are charged a penalty if a partnership tax return is late.
scope.excluded: No liability to a late filing penalty arises where the taxpayer shows a reasonable excuse (HMRC manual SALF208A, para 23) — but an insufficiency of funds is not a reasonable excuse unless attributable to events outside the taxpayer's control, and reliance on another person is not a reasonable excuse unless the taxpayer took reasonable care to avoid the failure. Daily £10 penalties are not automatic: they are not due unless HMRC decides a daily penalty should be payable and gives notice to the taxpayer. Separately, these fixed penalties do NOT apply to taxpayers within Making Tax Digital for Income Tax for the tax years they are in MTD — they get a points-based regime instead (£200 at 4 points). The MTD penalties also do not apply to non-resident company returns, trust or estate returns, or partnership returns.
scope.from_when: Schedule 55 Finance Act 2009, in force for returns from 2010/11 onwards. For someone joining MTD for Income Tax on 6 April 2026, the penalties on this entry still apply to the 2025/26 return due 31 January 2027; the MTD points system applies from the 2026/27 return onwards.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — the £100 and the 6/12-month penalties arise automatically and HMRC issues a penalty notice. To challenge one, appeal to HMRC on the ground of reasonable excuse (form SA370 or online); appeals go on to the First-tier Tribunal and Upper Tribunal.

notes: Verified at both the gov.uk guidance page and HMRC manual SALF208A. SALF208A does NOT state any cap limiting the penalty to the tax liability. The MTD for Income Tax change is the live risk on this subject: anyone mandated into MTD from 6 April 2026 moves to the points system for their 2026/27 return (due 31 January 2028), so content must be clear which year it describes.

title: Self Assessment Late Payment Penalties and Interest

figures.what: late payment penalty where tax is still unpaid 30 days after the due date (HMRC manual: arises automatically, equal to 5% of the tax unpaid at that date)
further late payment penalty at 6 months (HMRC manual: tax unpaid after the end of the period of 5 months beginning with the penalty date)
further late payment penalty at 12 months (HMRC manual: tax unpaid after the end of the period of 11 months beginning with the penalty date)
HMRC late payment interest rate in force on 14 November 2026 (effective from 9 January 2026)
HMRC late payment interest rate taking effect from 24 November 2026 (NOT yet in force on 14 November 2026)
HMRC repayment interest rate in force on 14 November 2026 (effective from 9 January 2026); rises to 3.00% from 24 November 2026

figures.value: Bank of England base rate plus 4 percentage points
figures.what: how the HMRC late payment interest rate is set (since 6 April 2025); repayment interest is base rate minus 1 percentage point, with a 0.5% lower limit

scope.who: Self Assessment taxpayers who do not pay the tax shown as due on their return (including Capital Gains Tax and student loan repayments) by the due date. Three separate 5% penalties can arise — at 30 days, 6 months and 12 months late — and interest is charged on the amount owed in addition to the penalties, running daily from the due date.
scope.excluded: No liability to a late payment penalty arises where the taxpayer satisfies HMRC that there is a reasonable excuse (HMRC manual SALF308A, para 16) — but an insufficiency of funds is not a reasonable excuse unless attributable to events outside the taxpayer's control, and reliance on another person is not a reasonable excuse unless the taxpayer took reasonable care. These 5% penalties do NOT apply to taxpayers within Making Tax Digital for Income Tax for the tax years they are in MTD: they instead face 3% of the tax owed at day 15 plus 3% at day 30 plus 10% a year charged daily from day 31 (rising to 4% + 4% + 10% for 2027/28), with no penalty at all up to 15 days late and a 30-day grace period in the first year. Under the MTD regime penalties do not apply to payments on account. Interest, by contrast, is NOT a penalty and has no reasonable-excuse escape; it continues to run on unpaid tax and is unchanged by MTD. Penalties can also be avoided by agreeing a Time to Pay arrangement with HMRC before they arise.
scope.from_when: Schedule 56 Finance Act 2009, in force for 2010/11 onwards. The interest rate of 7.75% has applied since 9 January 2026; 8.00% applies from 24 November 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — penalties and interest arise automatically. To challenge a penalty, appeal to HMRC on reasonable-excuse grounds (form SA370 or online). To avoid further late payment penalties, set up a Time to Pay arrangement.

notes: IMPORTANT DATING: as at 14 November 2026 the live late payment interest rate is 7.75%; the gov.uk page also lists 8.00% effective from 24 November 2026, so any copy published on or after 24 November 2026 must say 8.00%. The rates page was last updated 6 November 2026. SALF308A frames the three penalties as 30 days / 5 months after the penalty date / 11 months after the penalty date, which is the same as gov.uk's 30 days / 6 months / 12 months. SALF308A does NOT exclude payments on account from the pre-MTD 5% penalties — it states the first penalty applies where 'a balancing payment or payment on account is still unpaid more than 30 days from the due date for that year's balancing payment', so unpaid payments on account can attract it; by contrast the MTD penalty guidance does exclude payments on account. Do not blur the two regimes in copy.

title: HMRC Budget Payment Plan

figures.what: the payment frequencies available under a Budget Payment Plan; you choose the frequency and the amount
how long you can pause payments under the plan if you need to

figures.value: 11 characters (your UTR followed by the letter K)
figures.what: the payment reference needed to set the plan up

scope.who: Self Assessment taxpayers who are up to date with their payments and want to pay towards their NEXT tax bill in advance by weekly or monthly Direct Debit. Payments are credited against the next bill, so there is less to pay at the payment deadline. Payments can be paused for up to 6 months. If the amount paid does not cover the whole of the next bill, the difference must still be paid by the deadline; if the account is in credit, a refund can be requested.
scope.excluded: You cannot set up a Budget Payment Plan unless you are up to date with any payments from your last Self Assessment tax bill — gov.uk states 'To set up a plan you must be up to date with any payments from your last Self Assessment tax bill.' It is therefore not available to anyone with an outstanding or overdue balance from their last bill, and it is not a route for paying off an overdue bill at all: anyone who has missed a Self Assessment payment deadline or cannot pay what they owe needs a Time to Pay arrangement instead. It also requires a Self Assessment online account and a Direct Debit, so it is not open to anyone who cannot or will not pay by Direct Debit.
scope.from_when: Standing HMRC facility, available now; payments count towards the next Self Assessment bill.
scope.how_to_claim: Sign in to your Self Assessment online account, select 'Direct Debit' and choose the Budget Payment Plan option, then decide whether to pay weekly or monthly and how much. You will need your 11-character payment reference (your UTR followed by the letter K).

notes: The gov.uk page lists only the one eligibility condition (being up to date with the last bill) — no minimum or maximum payment amount and no debt threshold are stated at primary source, so content must not invent one. The distinction from Time to Pay is drawn by the page's own structure (Budget Payment Plan = paying ahead while up to date; Time to Pay = an overdue bill you cannot pay) rather than by a single explicit sentence. Note a naming inconsistency on gov.uk itself: the page heading is 'Pay weekly or monthly' and the scheme is written 'Budget Payment plan' in the body.

title: Self Assessment Time to Pay Payment Plan

figures.what: maximum Self Assessment debt that can be arranged as an online payment plan without contacting HMRC directly; those owing more can still apply but must contact HMRC
the longest period over which the online Self Assessment payment plan spreads the payments
a Time to Pay arrangement cannot be set up until the Self Assessment return has been filed

scope.who: Self Assessment taxpayers who cannot pay their tax bill in full and who have already filed the return. A plan spreads the overdue amount into regular monthly instalments and, while it is kept to, avoids further late payment penalties. HMRC checks that the plan is affordable; where there are savings or assets, HMRC expects those to be used to reduce the debt as much as possible first. A missed instalment incurs interest as well as a penalty.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the ONLINE self-serve payment plan and must contact HMRC directly if: you owe more than £30,000; you need longer than 12 months to pay; or you have not yet filed your Self Assessment tax return (HMRC: 'A Time to Pay arrangement cannot be set up until a Self Assessment return has been filed'). Companies in tax debt face extra questions and are expected to reduce the debt as much as possible before a plan is set up. A payment plan is also not a route for a bill that is not yet due — paying ahead of the deadline is a Budget Payment Plan instead. Interest continues to run on the outstanding balance throughout a Time to Pay arrangement.
scope.from_when: Standing HMRC facility, available now; the current £30,000 online threshold was confirmed in HMRC's gov.uk release of 9 December 2025.
scope.how_to_claim: File the return first, then check eligibility and set the plan up through the 'Set up a Self Assessment payment plan' online service via gov.uk. If you cannot set one up online — because you owe more than £30,000, need longer than 12 months, or are otherwise ineligible — contact HMRC to agree a plan.

scope.who: Anyone who needs to complete a Self Assessment tax return for a tax year and has either never sent a tax return before, or registered before but did not need to send a return for the previous year. They must tell HMRC by 5 October following the end of that tax year — six months from the end of the tax year in which the liability arises. Penalties for failure to notify are a percentage of the tax unpaid, set by whether the failure was non-deliberate, deliberate, or deliberate and concealed, and reduced for unprompted disclosure and for disclosure within 12 months of the tax becoming due.
scope.excluded: HMRC manual SALF210 sets out the statutory exceptions to the requirement to notify (s.7(3) to (7)): a taxpayer is excepted where they have no chargeable gains, or their chargeable gains do not exceed the annual exempt amount, AND either they have no net liability to income tax for the year, or they have had sufficient tax deducted at source to meet their net income tax liability for the year. Anyone who has already been sent a notice to file, or who registered and filed for the previous year, does not need to re-register. On penalties: HMRC states 'If you have a reasonable excuse for a non-deliberate failure to notify, we won't charge you a penalty', provided the failure was not deliberate and HMRC was told without unreasonable delay once the excuse ended. There is also no failure-to-notify penalty where no tax is unpaid, since the penalty is a percentage of the unpaid tax.
scope.from_when: Standing rule under s.7 Taxes Management Act 1970; failure to notify penalties under Schedule 41 Finance Act 2008. The live gov.uk page currently states the 5 October 2026 deadline for the 2025/26 tax year; the deadline for the 2026/27 tax year is 5 October 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Use the 'Check how to register for Self Assessment' service on gov.uk to register and get a Unique Taxpayer Reference. gov.uk warns: 'If you tell HMRC after 5 October 2026, you could get a penalty.'

notes: DATING WARNING for the content team: the gov.uk registration page is written dynamically around 'the previous tax year', and as read on 14 November 2026 it shows the 5 October 2026 deadline for 2025/26 — a date that has already passed. Copy should give the rule ('by 5 October following the end of the tax year') and the concrete 5 October 2027 date for 2026/27 rather than lifting the page's current year wording. Note also that gov.uk says only 'you could get a penalty' and does not quantify it; the percentages come from HMRC factsheet CC/FS11. The penalty is a percentage of the tax unpaid, not a fixed sum — do not present it as a flat fee. The gov.uk page's second registration trigger is worded against 'the tax year 2024 to 2025', which appears to lag the page's own 2025/26 framing; treat that detail as unreliable and do not reproduce the year.

scope.who: All UK VAT-registered businesses on standard (normally quarterly) accounting periods that file the return online and pay electronically: the return and the cleared payment are both due one calendar month and 7 days after the end of the accounting period. A return is due for every period even if there is no VAT to pay or reclaim.
scope.excluded: Payment on Account businesses and Annual Accounting Scheme businesses do not get the 7-day extension to either the return or the payment (VATAC1300); an annual return carries two months rather than one month. Businesses paying by cheque by post get no 7-day extension at all: the cheque is late unless it clears by the standard due date, even though the online return displays the extended date. Nil and repayment paper returns from businesses exempt from online filing must arrive by the standard due date.
scope.from_when: Current rule as read on 14 November 2026. Return due date set by regulation 25(1) and payment due date by regulation 40(2) of the VAT Regulations 1995; the 7-day online extension is given by HMRC Direction under regulations 25A(20) and 40(3) and (4).
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. The deadline applies automatically, and the 7-day extension applies automatically where the return is filed online and the payment is made electronically. The extended date appears on the return itself.

notes: There is no extension where the deadline falls on a weekend or bank holiday — the return and the cleared payment must arrive on or before the deadline (gov.uk/submit-vat-return). Faster Payments can be received on weekends and bank holidays. No Northern Ireland difference for deadlines: the rule is UK-wide.

scope.who: VAT-registered businesses whose taxable turnover excluding VAT is expected to be £150,000 or less in the next year. A business whose spending on relevant goods (including VAT) is under 2% of its flat rate turnover, or over 2% but under £1,000 a year, is a limited cost business and must use the 16.5% rate instead of its trade sector rate.
scope.excluded: You cannot join if: you are not registered for VAT; you use the second-hand margin scheme or the auctioneers' scheme; you are required to use the Tour Operator's Margin Scheme; you are required to operate the Capital Goods Scheme for certain capital items; you stopped using the Flat Rate Scheme in the 12 months before the date of your new application; in the last 12 months you accepted a compound penalty offer or were convicted of an offence in connection with VAT; in the last 12 months you were assessed with a penalty for conduct involving dishonesty; you are, or in the last 24 months were, registered in a VAT group or as a division, or are eligible to join a VAT group (para 3.7); or your business is 'associated' with another one in the way set out in para 3.8. HMRC may waive the group and association restrictions in writing. You must also leave once total VAT-inclusive income exceeds £230,000.
scope.from_when: Current rule as read on 14 November 2026. Apply from the start of a VAT accounting period.
scope.how_to_claim: Must be applied for. Apply online, by post or by email (VAT Notice 733 para 2.6). If already VAT-registered, apply on form VAT600FRS (para 5.1); if joining when you register for VAT, apply as part of the registration.

notes: The £150,000 join limit is VAT-exclusive taxable turnover; the £230,000 leave limit is VAT-inclusive total income including exempt supplies — the two figures are measured on different bases, which is the most common error in commentary on this scheme. The 16.5% limited cost rate and the 2%/£1,000 test are stated in VAT Notice 733 section 4.4, not on the short gov.uk overview page. No Northern Ireland difference in the turnover limits or rates.

title: VAT Cash Accounting Scheme

figures.what: Estimated VAT taxable turnover, excluding VAT, expected in the next 12 months — the limit to join the scheme (VAT Notice 731 section 2.1)
Join limit as stated on the gov.uk eligibility page
Annual value of taxable supplies excluding VAT, over a 12-month period, above which you must leave the scheme (VAT Notice 731 sections 2.5 and 6.2)

scope.who: VAT-registered businesses expecting taxable supplies excluding VAT of £1.35 million or less in the next year. You account for VAT on sales when your customers pay you, and reclaim VAT on purchases when you have paid your supplier.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the scheme if: your expected taxable supplies for the next year exceed £1.35 million; you have VAT Returns outstanding; within the last year you were convicted of a VAT offence, accepted an offer to compound proceedings, or were assessed to a penalty for dishonest VAT evasion; you owe HMRC money and have no arrangement to clear it; HMRC withdrew your use of the scheme or denied you access within the last year; or you cannot meet the record-keeping requirements (VAT Notice 731 section 6.2). You also cannot combine it with the Flat Rate Scheme (section 2.8). Separately, specific supplies are outside the scheme and must be accounted for under normal VAT rules: goods bought or sold under lease purchase, hire purchase, conditional sale or credit sale agreements; goods imported or acquired from an EU member state, or removed from a customs warehouse or free zone; certain goods and services subject to a domestic reverse charge; supplies where payment of an issued VAT invoice is not due in full within 6 months; and supplies where you issue a VAT invoice before making the supply (sections 2.7, 2.8, 5.5).
scope.from_when: Current rule as read on 14 November 2026. You can start from the beginning of your next VAT accounting period; new registrants can use the scheme from their date of registration (VAT Notice 731 section 3.2). You cannot apply the scheme retrospectively.
scope.how_to_claim: No application and no notification to HMRC. VAT Notice 731 section 3.1 states there is no need to apply to use the scheme; you simply start using it at the beginning of a VAT accounting period if you are eligible, and the gov.uk join page confirms you do not have to tell HMRC you use cash accounting. You should leave at the end of a VAT accounting period.

notes: Northern Ireland difference: goods imported into Northern Ireland from the EU are outside the scheme and must be accounted for under normal VAT rules (gov.uk eligibility page; VAT Notice 731 section 2.7). A one-off breach of the £1.6 million limit does not force you out if the increase has not happened before and is not expected to recur (for example selling a capital asset), it arose from genuine commercial activity, and you have reasonable grounds to expect taxable supplies below £1.35 million over the next 12 months — you must record the decision (VAT Notice 731 section 2.6). If turnover exceeded £1.35 million in the last 3 months, outstanding VAT must be reported and paid straight away (gov.uk join/leave page).

scope.who: VAT-registered businesses expecting taxable supplies of up to £1,350,000 (excluding VAT, exempt supplies and capital asset sales). You submit one VAT Return a year instead of four, pay nine monthly instalments of 10% of the previous year's liability by default — or three quarterly instalments of 25% in months 4, 7 and 10 on request — and then make a balancing payment or claim a refund with the annual return.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the scheme if: you are registered for VAT as part of a company group or as a division; you stopped using annual accounting in the previous 12 months; your business is insolvent; or you have a growing VAT debt (a small debt with agreed repayment proposals may still allow entry) (VAT Notice 732 section 2.6). You must also leave once taxable supplies exceed £1,600,000 per year.
scope.from_when: Current rule as read on 14 November 2026. Where a part-year accounting period is under 4 months, the return and balancing payment are due 1 month rather than 2 months after the period end (VAT Notice 732 section 3.6).
scope.how_to_claim: Must be applied for on form VAT600AA (VAT Notice 732 sections 8.1 and 8.2). If you are not yet VAT-registered you can register and apply at the same time. To use annual accounting alongside the Flat Rate Scheme, complete both VAT600AA and VAT600FRS (section 9.1).

notes: Annual Accounting Scheme businesses do not get the 7-day online filing and electronic payment extension that applies to standard quarterly returns (HMRC VAT Accounting manual VATAC1300, read 2026-11-14) — the annual return and balancing payment are due 2 months after the year end. Annual Accounting instalments are also outside the late payment penalty regime (gov.uk late payment penalties guidance, read 2026-11-14). No Northern Ireland difference in the limits or instalment pattern.

scope.who: All UK VAT-registered businesses, for VAT accounting periods starting on or after 1 January 2023. One penalty point is awarded for each late return until the frequency threshold is reached; at the threshold a £200 penalty is charged, and another £200 for each further late return while you remain at the threshold. Nil returns and repayment returns are covered. Late payment penalties apply to any VAT not paid in full by the due date.
scope.excluded: No penalty point is given for: your first VAT Return after becoming newly VAT registered; your final VAT Return after cancelling your registration; and one-off returns covering a period other than a month, a quarter or a year. For periods starting on or before 31 December 2022 the old VAT default surcharge applies instead, not this regime. The late payment penalties do not apply to payments on account or to Annual Accounting Scheme instalments (gov.uk late payment penalties guidance).
scope.from_when: Points-based regime: VAT accounting periods starting on or after 1 January 2023. Current late payment penalty rates of 3% / further 3% / 10% per annum: from 1 April 2025.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — points and penalties are issued automatically by HMRC. Points can be adjusted when you change accounting periods, and those adjustments cannot be appealed. Separate HMRC guidance covers removing penalty points.

notes: Submitting on time once at the threshold keeps you at the threshold without a further £200 charge; it does not clear the points. Late payment interest is charged separately, from the first day the payment is overdue until it is paid in full, in addition to any late payment penalty. The second late payment penalty runs from day 31 until the balance is paid or just before the 2-year assessment time limit. No Northern Ireland difference. The 1 April 2025 commencement of the higher rates is not stated on the gov.uk late payment penalties guidance page itself — its update history only records on 10 July 2025 that 'the value of late payment penalties charged has been increased' — so the date is cited to the HMRC policy publication instead.

title: VAT domestic reverse charge for building and construction services

figures.what: The charge applies to invoices with a tax point on or after this date; earlier tax points follow the normal VAT rules
The end user disregard: a predominantly end-user customer may re-supply a very small share of the services and still issue an end user declaration

scope.who: Supplies of standard-rated and reduced-rated building and construction services where the customer is VAT registered in the UK, the supply is reported within the Construction Industry Scheme (CIS), the supplier is not an employment business, and the customer has not given written confirmation that it is an end user or an intermediary supplier. The customer, not the supplier, accounts for the VAT on its own VAT Return.
scope.excluded: The charge does not apply where: the customer has notified the supplier in writing that it is an end user — a VAT and CIS registered business or group that does not make onward supplies of the construction services it receives (ending the reverse charge is optional for an end user); the customer is an intermediary supplier that has notified the supplier in writing — a VAT and CIS registered business re-supplying the services without material change to a connected or linked end user, connection being a relevant interest in the same land such as landlord and tenant, or membership of the same corporate group under section 1161 Companies Act 2006; the customer is not VAT registered, including private domestic customers; the supply is zero-rated (standard-rated items within a zero-rated supply of construction services, such as ovens and hobs, are excluded, as is scaffolding for a zero-rated construction project); the supplier is an employment business supplying staff or workers; or the supply is outside CIS. Specified services supplied on their own are also outside the charge: drilling for or extracting oil or natural gas; mineral extraction and related tunnelling, boring or underground works; manufacturing or delivering to site building or engineering components, equipment, materials, plant or machinery; manufacturing or delivering to site components for heating, lighting, air-conditioning, ventilation, power, drainage, sanitation, water supply or fire protection systems; professional work of architects or surveyors, or of building, engineering, interior, exterior decoration and landscape consultants; making, installing or repairing purely artistic works such as sculptures and murals; signwriting and erecting, installing or repairing signboards and advertisements; installing seating, blinds and shutters; and installing security systems such as burglar alarms, CCTV and public address systems. Where the charge does not apply, normal VAT rules apply.
scope.from_when: Tax points on or after 1 March 2021. Transitional rules apply to authenticated tax receipts and self-billed invoices.
scope.how_to_claim: The charge applies automatically where the conditions are met — it is not claimed. To disapply it, the customer must notify the supplier in writing that it is an end user or intermediary supplier: by post, by email, or within a contract the customer agrees to. The notice should be kept with normal business records and should make clear which supplies it covers. An intermediary supplier may describe itself as an end user in that notice. If the notification is invalid, the customer must account for the VAT that should have been charged under the reverse charge.

notes: The start date and the end user / intermediary supplier exceptions are not on the main 'Check when you must use' page — that page's main text gives no effective date and has no end user section, so both are cited to the HMRC VAT domestic reverse charge technical guide. The main page's update history records only that the start was moved from 1 October 2020 to 1 March 2021. The charge is UK-wide including Northern Ireland; no NI-specific difference was found at primary source. Note the interaction with the Cash Accounting Scheme: certain goods and services subject to a domestic reverse charge are outside cash accounting (VAT Notice 731 section 2.8).

scope.who: All employers operating PAYE anywhere in the UK must send an FPS on or before each payday, reporting employees' pay, payrolled benefits and deductions. Penalties are charged per PAYE scheme, so an employer running more than one scheme can be charged for each.
scope.excluded: No late filing penalty is charged where: all reported payments on the FPS are within 3 days of payday; it is the employer's first failure in the tax year to send a report on time (this exception does NOT apply to employers registered as an annual scheme); or a new employer sent its first FPS within 30 days of paying an employee. Where a permitted exception applies and the FPS is sent after payday, the employer must enter a late reporting reason on the FPS. scope.who: Employees who have an employment contract, have done some work under that contract, have been sick for at least one full working day (a 'period of incapacity for work'), and give their employer notice and proof of illness when needed. From 6 April 2026 it is available to all eligible employees regardless of earnings. Agency workers may be entitled. The employer pays it through payroll for the employee's qualifying days.
scope.excluded: Employees who: have already received the maximum 28 weeks of SSP; are getting Statutory Maternity Pay or Maternity Allowance; are off work for a pregnancy-related illness in the 4 weeks before the week (Sunday to Saturday) the baby is due; were in custody or on strike on the first day of sickness (including any linked periods); are working outside the EU where the employer is not liable for their National Insurance contributions; or received Employment and Support Allowance within 12 weeks of starting or returning to work for that employer. Also excluded are employees with a continuous series of linked periods lasting more than 3 years, and anyone who is not an employee (no employment contract). An employee who fails to tell the employer within the notification deadline may lose some SSP.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 (rate and the removal of waiting days and the earnings test)
scope.how_to_claim: The employee must tell their employer they cannot work, usually by the employer's own deadline, or within 7 days if the employer has not set one, and provide proof of illness when required. The employer then pays SSP through payroll — the employee does not claim from HMRC. If the employee does not qualify, the employer must send form SSP1 within 7 days of the first day off sick. If SSP ends unexpectedly while the employee is still sick, SSP1 must be sent within 7 days of SSP ending; if SSP is expected to end before the sickness does, SSP1 must be sent on or before the beginning of the 23rd week.

notes: The SSP reform took effect on 6 April 2026: waiting days are abolished and the earnings test removed, with the rate now the lower of £123.25 a week and 80% of average weekly earnings. HMRC's employer rates page and the transitional guidance both present this UK-wide without a nation caveat. I verified the rate and the removal of waiting days only on those UK-wide HMRC pages; I did not separately verify Northern Ireland's devolved legislative position, so NI-specific content should be checked before publication. Daily SSP amounts depend on the number of qualifying days the employee works each week. UK-wide, so valid for Birmingham/West Midlands and for Romanian-speaking audiences across the UK. Where income tax arises in related content, Scotland sets its own income tax rates and bands.

scope.who: Employees who have been continuously employed by the same employer for at least 26 weeks continuing into the qualifying week (the 15th week before the expected week of childbirth), are on the employer's payroll in that qualifying week, have average weekly earnings at or above the Lower Earnings Limit applying at the end of the qualifying week, are still pregnant at the 11th week before the due week or have had the baby by then, have stopped working, have an employer in the UK with earnings attracting Class 1 National Insurance liability, and give the correct notice and medical evidence. scope.excluded: Employees who fail any of those conditions are not entitled: those with less than 26 weeks' continuous employment into the qualifying week; those not on the payroll in the qualifying week; those whose average weekly earnings are below the Lower Earnings Limit at the end of the qualifying week; those who do not give the required notice; and those who do not supply evidence of the due or birth date (the employer does not have to pay SMP if proof has not been received 13 weeks after the SMP start date). Anyone who is not an employee of a UK employer — including the self-employed — is excluded; they may be able to claim Maternity Allowance instead. Employees not entitled to SMP may be able to get Maternity Allowance. scope.who: Employers must deduct student loan and postgraduate loan repayments through payroll from employees who are repaying, on earnings above the relevant plan threshold, at 9% (Plans 1, 2, 4 and 5) or 6% (Postgraduate Loan). Which plan applies depends on the funding body the borrower applied to and when their course started: Plan 1 — Student Finance England or Wales, course started before 1 September 2012, and Student Finance Northern Ireland (undergraduate or postgraduate); Plan 2 — Student Finance England for courses started 1 September 2012 to 31 July 2023 (undergraduate, PGCE, Advanced Learner Loans, short course loans), England for Higher Education Short Course Loans started on or after 1 August 2023, and Student Finance Wales for courses started on or after 1 September 2012 (undergraduate and PGCE); Plan 4 — Student Awards Agency Scotland (undergraduate or postgraduate); Plan 5 — Student Finance England for courses started on or after 1 August 2023 (undergraduate, PGCE, Advanced Learner Loans, Lifelong Learning Entitlement finance); Postgraduate Loan — master's or doctoral courses funded by England or Wales.
scope.excluded: No deduction is due on earnings at or below the relevant plan threshold. Employers are not responsible for deducting student or postgraduate loan repayments for off-payroll workers engaged through their own companies. Recipients of occupational pensions are not liable for student loan or postgraduate loan deductions. No deductions are made from payments made after an employee's date of death. Employers must stop deducting on receipt of an SL2 or PGL2 stop notice from HMRC, or when HMRC tells them to stop in writing. An employee cannot ask the employer to stop deductions — HMRC is explicit that 'You cannot stop making deductions because your employee asks you to'; an employee who thinks they have overpaid must request a refund instead.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim. Deductions are made automatically through payroll from the next available payday once the employer receives an SL1 or PGL1 start notice from HMRC, or where a new employee's P45 shows deductions should continue, or where a new employee tells the employer they are repaying a student loan. If the employee does not know which plan they are on, HMRC says to use Plan 5 until an SL1 notice is received. On an employee leaving, enter 'Y' in P45 box 5 even if the employee had not earned enough to make repayments.

notes: Plan 4 is the Scottish student loan plan — borrowers who applied through the Student Awards Agency Scotland. Plan 5 is the England-only plan for courses starting on or after 1 August 2023. Plan 1 is where Northern Ireland borrowers sit. Plan 2 covers Wales (from 1 September 2012) and the England 2012–2023 cohort. The thresholds and rates themselves are UK-wide payroll figures and apply identically to employers in Birmingham and the West Midlands and to Romanian-speaking employees anywhere in the UK, so the brand tags are correct even though the plan a borrower sits on depends on their funding nation. HMRC's rates page gives a single 9% rate for Plans 1, 2, 4 and 5 rather than a separate rate per plan, and 6% for the Postgraduate Loan. An employee can be repaying a student loan and a postgraduate loan at the same time, in which case both deductions run. Where income tax is relevant, Scotland sets its own income tax rates and bands. scope.who: Individuals who are taxpayers in England, Wales or Northern Ireland for the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. The Personal Allowance of £12,570 itself is UK-wide and applies to Scottish taxpayers too; the 20%/40%/45% rates and the £37,700 basic rate limit shown here apply to non-savings, non-dividend income of taxpayers in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Savings and dividend income is taxed at UK-wide rates for taxpayers in all four nations.
scope.excluded: Scottish taxpayers do not get these bands and rates on their non-savings, non-dividend income — Scotland has its own starter (19%), basic (20%), intermediate (21%), higher (42%), advanced (45%) and top (48%) rates and its own thresholds. Anyone with adjusted net income of £125,140 or more gets no Personal Allowance at all, because of the taper. Dividend income is taxed at the separate dividend rates, not at 20/40/45%. Companies are outside income tax entirely (they pay Corporation Tax).
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: No claim needed. The Personal Allowance is given automatically through your PAYE tax code or in your Self Assessment calculation. The £100,000 taper is applied automatically by HMRC, but if your income is near or above £100,000 you may need to file a Self Assessment return or tell HMRC about changes in income so your code is right; a wrong code means an under- or overpayment to settle later.

notes: Income tax rates and bands on non-savings, non-dividend income are DEVOLVED to Scotland: the Scottish Parliament sets its own rates and thresholds, so this is not a UK-wide band structure and must not be presented as one. Wales has Welsh rates of income tax, but HMRC publishes Welsh rates together with England and Northern Ireland for 2026/27 at the same 20/40/45%. The Personal Allowance (£12,570), the £100,000 income limit, and the savings and dividend rates are reserved and UK-wide. Budget 2026 confirms the Personal Allowance, basic rate limit and £100,000 income limit are unchanged for 2027-28 as well; the maintained-thresholds policy runs to 5 April 2031.

scope.who: UK-resident individuals disposing of chargeable assets in the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027 — shares outside an ISA, second homes and buy-to-lets, business assets, crypto, valuables and so on. Also personal representatives of a deceased person and trustees, at their own exempt amounts and rates. CGT is reserved, so the same exempt amount and rates apply across England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland (including for Scottish taxpayers, whose Scottish bands do not change the CGT rate bands).
scope.excluded: Companies do not pay CGT — they pay Corporation Tax on chargeable gains and get no annual exempt amount. Trustees other than trustees for disabled people get £1,500, not £3,000. Gains on your own home are normally not chargeable at all because of Private Residence Relief, and gains on assets inside an ISA or a pension are exempt, so no exempt amount is used. The £3,000 is per person per tax year, is not transferable between spouses or civil partners, and cannot be carried forward if unused. Non-UK residents are generally outside the charge except on disposals of UK land and property and certain UK-property-rich company interests. Gifts and transfers between spouses or civil partners living together are on a no-gain-no-loss basis, so no exempt amount is used.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: The £3,000 annual exempt amount is applied automatically in the tax calculation — there is nothing to claim. You do have to report and pay: residential property disposals must be reported and the tax paid within 60 days of completion using HMRC's UK Property Account service, and other chargeable gains are reported either on a Self Assessment return or through HMRC's real-time Capital Gains Tax service. Reliefs such as Business Asset Disposal Relief must be claimed separately.

notes: Since 30 October 2024 the main CGT rates have been aligned with the residential property rates, so for 2026/27 residential property and other chargeable assets are both taxed at 18% within the basic rate band and 24% above it — there is no longer a higher separate residential rate. The 18%/24% split depends on your total taxable income: gains are stacked on top of income, and the part of the gain falling above the basic rate limit is taxed at 24%. Business Asset Disposal Relief rose to 18% for disposals on or after 6 April 2026 (it was 14% in 2025/26 and 10% before that), and Budget 2026 announced the BADR lifetime limit falls from £1 million to £500,000 from 2027-28 — that is a future change, not a 2026/27 one.

figures.what: Rent a Room Scheme tax-free threshold per year, per person

scope.who: Resident landlords letting furnished accommodation in their only or main home — owner-occupiers and tenants alike, so you can use it whether or not you own the property. It also covers taking in a lodger, and lettings that amount to a trade such as running a bed and breakfast or guest house or providing meals and cleaning. The threshold is per person, so two people each letting rooms in the same shared home have £3,750 each.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the scheme where the accommodation is not part of your main home at the time you let it; where the accommodation is not furnished; where a home has been converted into separate flats that are let; where the accommodation is let as an office or for any business (HMRC allows two exceptions — a lodger who works at home in the evenings or at weekends, and a student given study facilities); or on a UK home let out while you live abroad. You also cannot use the exemption or Method B to create a loss, and if you use Method B you cannot deduct expenses or capital allowances. You cannot claim the £1,000 property allowance on the same Rent a Room income.
scope.from_when: Scheme in force and applies for the 2026/27 tax year (6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027); the £7,500 limit has applied since 6 April 2016
scope.how_to_claim: If your gross receipts from the letting are £7,500 or less (£3,750 if shared) the exemption is automatic — you are exempt from tax on that income and need do nothing. If your receipts exceed the threshold you must complete a Self Assessment tax return and choose between Method A (tax on your actual profit, which HMRC applies by default) and Method B (tax on gross receipts above the threshold, with no deduction for expenses). To use Method B, or to opt out of the exemption so you can claim a loss, you must notify HMRC within one year of the 31 January following the end of the tax year. Method B stops automatically if your rental income falls back below the threshold.

notes: This is a UK-wide income tax relief, reserved to Westminster, so it applies in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland on the same terms. The £7,500 limit is a fixed statutory figure, not an annually indexed one, and has been unchanged since April 2016 — it is not restated in Budget rates tables, so verify it on the live guidance page each year. The threshold is on GROSS receipts, including any amounts your lodger pays for meals, cleaning or laundry, not on profit. The HS223 helpsheet carrying the fullest list of exclusions is the 2026-published version covering the 2025 to 2026 tax year; the £7,500 figure for the current year is taken from the live GOV.UK guidance page read on 14 November 2026.

title: Property Income Allowance

figures.what: property allowance — tax-free allowance per year for individuals with income from land or property
where you have both property income and trading income, a separate £1,000 allowance applies to each

scope.who: Individuals with gross income from UK or overseas land or property — a let room, a parking space, a holiday let, land. It is a per-person allowance, so where a property is jointly owned each owner can set their own £1,000 against their share of the gross rental income. It is separate from, and additional to, the £1,000 trading allowance: someone with both kinds of income gets £1,000 against each.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the property allowance against property income from a partnership in which you or a connected person are partners; against income from a company that you or a connected person owns or controls; or against income from your employer or from your spouse's or civil partner's employer. You cannot use it if you claim the tax reducer for residential finance costs such as mortgage interest. You cannot use it on income from letting a room in your own home under the Rent a Room Scheme, nor where you deduct expenses from that income instead of using the Rent a Room scheme. If you claim the allowance you cannot also deduct any other expenses or allowances against that income, and the allowance cannot create or increase a loss — so it is the wrong choice for a loss-making let. Companies cannot use it; it is an income tax allowance for individuals.
scope.from_when: Applies for the 2026/27 tax year (6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027); the allowance has applied since 6 April 2017
scope.how_to_claim: If your gross property income for the year is £1,000 or less the income is automatically exempt — you do not need to tell HMRC or declare it on a tax return, though you must keep records, and you can ask HMRC to stop issuing a return if you no longer need one. If your gross property income is more than £1,000 you must declare it, and you then choose on your Self Assessment return either to deduct the £1,000 allowance from your gross income instead of your actual expenses, or to work out your profit in the normal way by deducting actual expenses. It is a choice, so it is a claim rather than an automatic relief once you are above £1,000, and you should compare the two: the allowance only helps if your real expenses are less than £1,000.

notes: Distinct from the trading allowance, which is the same £1,000 amount but applies to casual self-employment and miscellaneous trading income; the two are separate allowances and a person with both types of income gets both. Also distinct from Rent a Room relief (£7,500) — you cannot use the property allowance on Rent a Room income, and for letting a furnished room in your own home Rent a Room relief is normally far more generous. The £1,000 is a fixed statutory figure, not indexed annually, and is not restated in Budget rates tables, so verify it on the live guidance page each year. The allowance applies to GROSS income before expenses. This is a reserved UK-wide income tax allowance.

scope.who: Members of UK registered pension schemes building up pension savings in the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. The allowance is the total that can be paid in across all your schemes in the year — your own contributions, employer contributions and tax relief, plus the deemed value of defined benefit build-up — before an annual allowance charge arises. Pension tax relief is reserved, so the £60,000 and the taper apply across England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland.
scope.excluded: You do not get the full £60,000 if the taper applies: where BOTH threshold income exceeds £200,000 and adjusted income exceeds £260,000, the allowance is reduced, down to a floor of £10,000 for the highest earners. You do not get the full allowance for money purchase savings if you have flexibly accessed a defined contribution pension — for example taking cash or a short-term annuity from a flexi-access drawdown fund, or taking cash from an uncrystallised pot — because the Money Purchase Annual Allowance of £10,000 then caps money purchase contributions and no carry forward is available against it. Separately, tax relief on your own personal contributions is capped at 100% of your relevant UK earnings (or £3,600 gross if you have little or no earnings), so a high annual allowance does not by itself permit a large relieved personal contribution. Companies are outside this: the annual allowance is a member-level limit, not an employer one.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: There is nothing to claim for the allowance itself — it is a cap, applied automatically. You do have responsibilities if you exceed it: your scheme must send you a pension savings statement if your savings in that scheme exceed the standard allowance, you can carry forward unused annual allowance from the previous three tax years (not against the MPAA), and if a charge is still due you must report the excess on a Self Assessment tax return and pay the annual allowance charge, or in some cases ask the scheme to pay it under 'scheme pays'. If you are a high earner you need to work out your own threshold and adjusted income to find your tapered allowance — HMRC provides a calculator and scheme administrators can check a member's allowance.

notes: UK-wide and reserved. The £60,000 standard allowance, the £10,000 MPAA, the £200,000/£260,000 taper thresholds and the £10,000 taper floor are all unchanged for 2026/27 and are confirmed unchanged for 2027-28 at Budget 2026. The main GOV.UK guidance page states the £60,000 and the two taper thresholds but gives no figure for the MPAA or the taper floor, so those two come from HMRC's pension schemes rates publication, which tabulates them by tax year. Note the taper requires BOTH income tests to be met, not either. Scotland: covered by the GOV.UK scheme (Scotland has its own disability benefits, which feed into UC elements, but the standard allowance is the same).

scope.nation: England, Wales and Northern Ireland. GOV.UK requires you to usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, and states that if you live in Scotland you cannot get the Winter Fuel Payment and may instead be eligible for Pension Age Winter Heating Payment.
scope.who: People born on or before 27 June 1960 who usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland during the qualifying week of 21 to 27 September 2026. Care home residents can get it, subject to the care home exclusion below. The amount depends on date of birth, who else eligible you live with, and whether you get Pension Credit, Universal Credit or income-related ESA.
scope.excluded: People who usually live in Scotland (Pension Age Winter Heating Payment instead) or outside England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Visitors who were in England, Wales or Northern Ireland during the qualifying week but usually live elsewhere. People in hospital getting free treatment for the whole qualifying week and the year before it. People who need permission to enter the UK and whose leave states they cannot claim public funds. People in prison for the whole qualifying week. Care home residents who both get Universal Credit, Pension Credit or income-related ESA and lived in a care home for the whole time from 29 June 2026 or earlier. And anyone whose total income is over £35,000 keeps nothing in the end: HMRC takes the payment back through the tax code or Self Assessment, so they can opt out instead.

scope.how_to_claim: Most eligible people get it automatically and receive a letter in October or November showing the amount. A claim is needed only if you do not get State Pension or one of the other listed benefits and either you have never had a Winter Fuel Payment before, or you have deferred your State Pension since your last one. Claims can be made by post from 21 September 2026 or by phone to the Winter Fuel Payment Centre from 19 October 2026, with a deadline of 31 March 2027. People with income over £35,000 can opt out instead of having it recovered.

notes: This is the area to be most careful with. Scotland: Winter Fuel Payment does not apply - GOV.UK states you cannot get it if you live in Scotland, where the devolved Pension Age Winter Heating Payment applies instead, so never present these amounts to a Scottish audience. Northern Ireland: unusually for a DWP benefit, Northern Ireland IS inside this scheme - the GOV.UK eligibility page lists England, Wales and Northern Ireland together. The £35,000 recovery rule is individual: GOV.UK says a partner's income does not count towards your total income, and recovery is usually through the PAYE tax code, or through Self Assessment where that applies; it cannot be repaid through Making Tax Digital software, so HMRC writes with the amount instead. Recheck set to 2027-01-15 because these rules and amounts have changed repeatedly in recent years and are winter-specific.

scope.nation: United Kingdom. scope.how_to_claim: Must be applied for - open a childcare account through the Tax-Free Childcare application on GOV.UK, then pay money in and the top-up is added. Check first that the childcare provider is signed up to the scheme.

Scotland: available, and the GOV.UK eligibility page lists Scottish Child Disability Payment and Adult Disability Payment as qualifying for the disabled-child route. scope.who: UK-resident companies and organisations chargeable to Corporation Tax. Profits of £50,000 or less are charged at the small profits rate of 19%; profits over £250,000 at the main rate of 25%; profits between £50,000 and £250,000 are charged at the main rate with Marginal Relief, which tapers the effective rate between 19% and 25%. Both limits are proportionately reduced for accounting periods of less than 12 months and divided by the number of associated companies plus one.
scope.excluded: Non-UK resident companies cannot claim Marginal Relief (gov.uk/guidance/corporation-tax-marginal-relief). Close investment-holding companies are excluded from both the small profits rate and Marginal Relief — CTA 2010 s.18N: close investment-holding companies "are chargeable at the CT main rate" and "are not eligible for the standard small profits rate or marginal relief" (HMRC CTM03951). Companies whose augmented profits, including certain distributions from unrelated, unassociated companies, exceed £250,000 get no Marginal Relief. Ring fence profits (UK/UK continental shelf oil rights or extraction) are outside the standard rates and have their own small ring fence profits rate of 19% with a ring fence fraction of 11/400 (CTM03910); CTA 2010 s.18A(1) applies the standard small profits rate only to profits "which are not ring fence profits". A company in liquidation is not treated as a close investment-holding company for the accounting period beginning when winding up commences, if it was not one in the prior period (CTA 2010 s.18N(5)).
scope.from_when: The two-rate structure with Marginal Relief applies from 1 April 2023. The rates and limits above are confirmed unchanged for the financial year beginning 1 April 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: No separate application. CTA 2010 s.18A(1) charges Corporation Tax at the standard small profits rate where the company is UK resident, is not a close investment-holding company, and its augmented profits do not exceed the lower limit. CTA 2010 s.18B(1) states "This section applies if—" the company is UK resident, is not a close investment-holding company, and its augmented profits exceed the lower limit but not the upper limit — so the relief operates as a statutory reduction rather than on application. The figures are self-assessed in the Company Tax Return; HMRC publishes a Marginal Relief calculator at gov.uk/guidance/corporation-tax-marginal-relief, which describes it as checking "how much Marginal Relief you may be able to claim".

notes: The GOV.UK guidance uses the language of claiming Marginal Relief, while the legislation (CTA 2010 ss.18A, 18B) frames both the small profits rate and the relief as applying automatically where the conditions are met — worth wording carefully in client copy. The associated-companies divisor is the commonest trap: a director with several companies loses the £50,000 band quickly. The gov.uk/corporation-tax-rates page itself does not mention the close investment-holding company exclusion; that comes from HMRC's Company Taxation Manual CTM03951 and CTA 2010 s.18N. CTM03910's published table runs to financial year 2025; FY2026 confirmation comes from the rates-and-allowances publication updated 1 April 2026.

Where a company's first accounts cover a period of more than 12 months, the first accounts are due within 21 months of incorporation (private) or 3 months from the accounting reference date, whichever is longer. Dormant companies have the same deadlines as other companies.
scope.excluded: The 9-month deadline does not apply to public companies, which have 6 months from the accounting reference date and 18 months from incorporation for a first set of accounts covering more than 12 months. The 21-month first-accounts rule does not apply where the first accounts cover 12 months or less — the normal deadlines then apply instead. Dormant companies are NOT excluded: they have the same filing deadlines as other companies and face the same late filing penalties. The Companies House accounts deadline is separate from, and does not replace, the 12-month Company Tax Return deadline or the 9-months-and-1-day Corporation Tax payment deadline.
scope.from_when: Current Companies House guidance as at 14 November 2026 (guidance page updated 23 October 2026). The deadlines themselves are long-standing and were not changed by the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act.

notes: ECCTA POSITION AS AT NOVEMBER 2026 — this is the material change worth banking. (1) The requirement for small companies and micro-entities to file a profit and loss account has been PAUSED. GOV.UK, 23 October 2026: "the government has decided to pause implementing the requirement for small and micro entities" — so as at November 2026 small companies "do not have to deliver a copy of the directors' report or the profit and loss account" and micro-entities are likewise not required to file "a directors' report or profit and loss account at Companies House" (life-of-a-company part 1, updated 23 October 2026). (2) ABRIDGED ACCOUNTS HAVE NOT BEEN ABOLISHED — the earlier plan to remove them has been reversed: the government will "continue to allow companies to file abridged accounts" (gov.uk/government/news/companies-house-update-to-accounts-filing-from-april-2028, published 23 October 2026). Where abridged accounts are filed, the balance sheet must state that the members have agreed to them. (3) What IS still coming from April 2028: all UK registered companies must "file their accounts in Inline eXtensible Business Reporting Language (iXBRL) format" using commercial software, and web and paper accounts filing closes on that date. Smaller companies keep the option to remove, or 'fillet', their profit and loss information from accounts filed after 1 April 2028. (4) The earlier 9 June 2026 notice announcing the P&L requirement and the removal of abridged accounts was WITHDRAWN on 23 October 2026 — do not cite it. (5) The ECCTA company accounts factsheet at gov.uk/government/publications/economic-crime-and-corporate-transparency-act-2023-factsheets/economic-crime-and-corporate-transparency-act-company-accounts still displays the old position (small and micro-entities must file a P&L, abridged accounts removed) and shows a visible date of 1 March 2024 with no commencement dates — it is out of date on these points and must not be used as the current position.

scope.who: Companies and unincorporated associations within the charge to Corporation Tax. Payment is due 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period; the Company Tax Return (CT600) is due 12 months after the end of the same accounting period — two different dates for the same period. A company or association must file a Company Tax Return if it receives a "notice to deliver a Company Tax Return" from HMRC, and must still send a return if it makes a loss or has no Corporation Tax to pay.
scope.excluded: The single 9-months-and-1-day payment date does not apply to companies with taxable profits above £1.5 million — they must pay Corporation Tax in instalments, with separate rules for profits between £1.5 million and £20 million and for profits above £20 million. People who are self-employed as a sole trader or in a partnership do not file a Company Tax Return at all and must file a Self Assessment return instead. A company that has told HMRC it is dormant for Corporation Tax will not need to file another Company Tax Return unless HMRC asks it to or it begins trading again.
scope.from_when: Long-standing; current GOV.UK guidance as read on 14 November 2026 (pay-corporation-tax page public update date 22 November 2024; company-tax-returns public update date 8 November 2024; deadlines table page updated 23 October 2026).
scope.how_to_claim: No claim. Both deadlines run automatically from the end of the accounting period. A company with no Corporation Tax to pay must still tell HMRC that it does not owe any by the 9-months-and-1-day date, and must still file the return by the 12-month date even if it made a loss.

notes: The counter-intuitive point for clients is that the tax is payable three months BEFORE the return that calculates it is due. Note also that the Corporation Tax accounting period is not necessarily the same as the Companies House accounting reference date period, so the three deadlines (Companies House accounts at 9 months, CT payment at 9 months and 1 day, CT600 at 12 months) are measured from dates that can differ.

scope.who: Sole traders, partnerships and limited companies investing in plant and machinery. AIA gives relief for most plant and machinery up to £1 million in the accounting period, pro-rated for periods that are not 12 months. Sole traders and partnerships with more than one business usually get one AIA per business, except where the businesses are under the same control and share either the same premises or similar activities, in which case they get only one.
scope.excluded: AIA cannot be claimed on: business cars (claim writing down allowances instead); "items you owned for another reason before you started using them in your business"; and "items given to you or your business". Mixed partnerships cannot claim at all — "AIA (annual investment allowance) is only available for partnerships where all the members are individuals", so a partnership with a corporate member is excluded. A business that is closing cannot claim AIA on items bought in its final accounting period. Sole traders and partnerships cannot claim the full value of an item also used outside the business — the claim is reduced by the private-use proportion. Two or more limited companies controlled by the same person get only one AIA between them, not one each.
scope.from_when: The £1 million limit is the permanent AIA amount (it was legislated at £1m rather than reverting to £200,000). Confirmed in force on the GOV.UK guide as read on 14 November 2026 (public update date 22 October 2024).
scope.how_to_claim: Must be claimed. GOV.UK: "Claim on your tax return." For a company, that is the Company Tax Return (CT600) for the accounting period in which the expenditure was incurred; for a sole trader or partnership, the Self Assessment return. The page links to separate guidance on how to claim capital allowances.

notes: The car exclusion is the single most common client misunderstanding: a van or a lorry is plant and machinery and qualifies, a car does not and goes into a writing down allowance pool instead. Zero-emission and electric cars sit under a separate first-year allowance regime (HMRC CA23153), not AIA — do not blur the two in copy. The common-control rule means a client with several companies has £1 million in total, not £1 million each. figures.value: no 'significant' transactions in the financial year

"Significant transactions do not include:" filing fees paid to Companies House; penalties for late filing of accounts; money paid for shares when the company was incorporated
an unincorporated association or club owing less than £100 Corporation Tax is usually dormant for Corporation Tax

figures.value: annual accounts and a confirmation statement

"Dormant company accounts submitted to Companies House do not need to include a profit and loss account"
dormant companies have the same accounts filing deadlines as other companies and face the same late filing penalties
a company dormant for Companies House that also qualifies as small can file dormant accounts and does not need an auditor's report

scope.who: A company or association "may be 'dormant' if it's not doing business ('trading') and does not have any other income". Dormant means two different things. For COMPANIES HOUSE, a company is dormant if it has had no significant transactions in the financial year; filing fees paid to Companies House, late filing penalties, and money paid for shares on incorporation do not count as significant. A company dormant for Companies House that also qualifies as small may file dormant accounts instead of full accounts and does not need an auditor's report, and those accounts need not include a profit and loss account. For CORPORATION TAX, a company is usually dormant if it has stopped trading and has no other income (for example investments), is a new limited company that has not yet started trading, is an unincorporated association or club owing less than £100 Corporation Tax, or is a flat management company.
scope.excluded: A company that has had any significant accounting transaction in the financial year is not dormant for Companies House — only filing fees, late filing penalties and share money paid at incorporation are disregarded, so a single bank charge, a bank interest receipt or any trading transaction breaks dormancy. A company that is dormant for Companies House but does not also qualify as small cannot file dormant accounts. Dormancy does not excuse filing: a dormant company must still file annual accounts and a confirmation statement, and must still file a Company Tax Return online if it has received a notice to deliver one. Being dormant for Corporation Tax does not make a company dormant for Companies House, or vice versa — the two tests are separate. A company registered for VAT that plans to restart trading must still send nil VAT returns while dormant.
scope.from_when: Current GOV.UK guidance as at 14 November 2026 (dormant-company overview, dormant-for-companies-house and dormant-for-corporation-tax pages all updated 23 October 2026; Companies House accounts guidance updated 23 October 2026).
scope.how_to_claim: Dormancy for Corporation Tax must be notified: tell HMRC using the online service at gov.uk/tell-hmrc-your-company-is-dormant-for-corporation-tax, or by phone or post via HMRC's Corporation Tax enquiries contact page. You need the company name, its 10-digit Unique Taxpayer Reference and the date it stopped trading if it traded; tax agents need an agent code. After telling HMRC, no further Company Tax Return is needed unless HMRC asks for one or the company begins trading again. Dormant accounts are filed with Companies House in the normal way, by the normal deadline.

notes: Two separate tests, two separate bodies, and clients routinely assume one notification covers both — it does not. Telling HMRC the company is dormant does nothing about the Companies House accounts and confirmation statement, which are still due on the normal timetable and attract the normal late filing penalties. The dormancy-breaking trap is that bank charges and bank interest are significant transactions, while the three disregarded items are narrow. The gov.uk/tell-hmrc-your-company-is-dormant-for-corporation-tax page does not itself define dormancy or mention notices to deliver — those come from gov.uk/dormant-company/dormant-for-corporation-tax, which should be the citation for the definition.

Selling online as well does not disqualify a shop, and requiring membership, tickets or appointments does not disqualify a venue.

The Schedule 1 excluded uses: financial services, medical and health services, professional services, warehouses used for online sales, certain business-use recording or film studios, crematoria, taxi firms, show homes, conference centres, betting shops, postal sorting offices, citizens advice bureaux, job centres, car parks and most public transport (bicycle docking stations are not excluded). notes: The headline for a 2026/27 client conversation is that the 40% RHL relief with its £110,000 cash cap has gone and been replaced by permanently lower multipliers with no cash cap — so a business comparing its 2026/27 bill with 2025/26 should look at transitional relief and the Supporting Small Business scheme, not at RHL relief. Claims for RHL relief for earlier years may still be made to the council. A separate Pubs and Live Music Venue Relief exists for 2026/27 in England (GOV.UK business rates information letter 3/2026); its percentage and cap were not reproduced on the letter and so are not reported here.
