scope.nation: England, Wales and Scotland (not Northern Ireland)
scope.who: England and Wales: the single 'core group' — on 23 August 2026 your electricity supplier was in the scheme, you or your partner received a qualifying means-tested benefit (Pension Credit including Savings Credit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Housing Benefit, or Universal Credit), and your or your partner's name was on the electricity bill. Scotland keeps two routes: a core group that gets the discount automatically (Pension Credit, certain Universal Credit or ESA premiums, or a Support for Mortgage Interest loan, and certain unemployed parents or carers of a child under 5), and a broader group who must apply to their electricity supplier. Park home residents who buy electricity from the site owner apply to a separate supplier-funded Park Homes scheme run by Charis Grants.
scope.excluded: Northern Ireland — GOV.UK states 'The Warm Home Discount scheme is not available in Northern Ireland' and points residents to the Affordable Warmth scheme. Scotland core group: automatic. Scotland broader group: you must apply to your electricity supplier, which sets extra criteria, and you should apply early because the number of discounts is limited and you must stay with that supplier until the discount is paid. scope.who: From the start of the 2026 to 2027 academic year, any child in a household receiving Universal Credit, whatever the household earns. Also eligible: households receiving support under Part VI of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, or the guarantee element of Pension Credit, and households meeting the separate 'no recourse to public funds' criteria. Children paid a qualifying benefit directly rather than through a parent or guardian qualify in their own right, as may a child below compulsory school age who is in full-time education. Separately, every pupil in reception, year 1 and year 2 at a state-funded school gets universal infant free school meals regardless of income. Students at DfE-funded further education institutions are entitled to free meals under separate criteria.
scope.excluded: Households receiving none of the qualifying benefits, apart from the universal infant entitlement for reception to year 2. Pupils who kept eligibility only through the transitional protections that ran from 1 April 2018: those ended at the close of the 2025 to 2026 academic year, so from the 2026 to 2027 academic year a household must actually meet the criteria to keep provision (such a pupil still counts in the 'Ever 6' cohort for school funding). Expanded free school meals cover the meal only and bring no disadvantage funding, so a Universal Credit household earning over £7,400 does not attract pupil premium. Children educated otherwise than at school (EOTAS) have no specific legal entitlement, and the local authority considers equivalent food provision case by case. The duty described in the guidance applies to maintained schools, academies, free schools, school-based and maintained nursery schools and non-maintained special schools, so independent schools are outside it. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run their own schemes and are not covered.
scope.from_when: The expanded Universal Credit entitlement is in force now, from the start of the 2026 to 2027 academic year (September 2026). GOV.UK's application page was last updated 27 October 2026 and states it.
scope.how_to_claim: Apply through your local authority — for a Birmingham reader, Birmingham City Council; GOV.UK routes applications through the council finder on its 'apply for free school meals' page. The claim must be made and verified by the school or local authority. Universal infant free school meals in reception to year 2 need no application, but GOV.UK still asks families on a qualifying benefit to apply, because a targeted eligibility check brings extra funding to the school. Families with no recourse to public funds should ask the school or local authority, as they may still be eligible.

notes: Two tiers now sit behind one meal: 'expanded' free school meals (any Universal Credit household) and 'targeted' free school meals (Universal Credit household earning £7,400 a year or less), and only the targeted tier carries pupil premium and other disadvantage funding — the distinction matters to schools' budgets, not to the child's meal. Eligible children also qualify for the Holiday Activities and Food programme. Scotland: mygov.scot. Wales: gov.wales. Northern Ireland: nidirect.gov.uk. Not verified in this pass: the further education free meals criteria, which GOV.UK holds in a separate guide.

scope.who: People more than 10 weeks pregnant, and parents or guardians with parental responsibility for at least one child under 4, who receive a qualifying benefit. Routes: Universal Credit with family take-home pay from employment of £408 a month or less (apply online); Pension Credit including the child addition (apply by email or phone); income-related Employment and Support Allowance, which can qualify a pregnant applicant though that route ends when the baby is born; anyone under 18 and more than 10 weeks pregnant, who qualifies with no benefit at all until the baby is born; and a non-British parent of one or more British children under 4 who has a no-recourse-to-public-funds condition or no immigration status, with family take-home pay of £408 a month or less. The money buys certain types of milk, infant formula, and fruit and vegetables, and claimants also get free Healthy Start vitamins.
scope.excluded: People living in Scotland — GOV.UK states 'If you live in Scotland you cannot get Healthy Start'; they apply for Best Start Foods instead. scope.from_when: Ongoing. Payments start from the 10th week of pregnancy; after the birth you must tell the scheme within 12 weeks of the due date to keep being paid.
scope.how_to_claim: You must apply. Online at the NHS Healthy Start website for the Universal Credit route; by email or phone for the Pension Credit route and for under-18s more than 10 weeks pregnant. Non-British parents who cannot claim public funds because of their immigration status request an application form by email. If you are under 10 weeks pregnant when you apply you can add the pregnancy later without a new application.

notes: Scotland is a genuine carve-out, not a variation: Best Start Foods is a separate Scottish Government scheme with its own amounts and rules, so Healthy Start figures must never be quoted to a Scottish reader. Free Healthy Start vitamins are arranged differently in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, so point readers at their own local arrangement. Buying from a dealer rather than a manufacturer does not stop an asset being unused, and limited testing, delivery or demonstration use does not either.
scope.excluded: Sole traders, partnerships and anyone not within the charge to Corporation Tax cannot claim. Cars are excluded — General exclusion 2: 'Expenditure incurred on the provision of a car is not eligible for full expensing or the 50% first-year allowance.' Plant or machinery bought for leasing is excluded — General exclusion 6: 'Expenditure on the provision of plant or machinery for leasing is excluded from the scope of full expensing' (with an exception for background plant or machinery in a building leased under an excluded lease). Second-hand or already-used assets are excluded. Expenditure that would be long-life asset expenditure but for transitional provisions is excluded under General exclusion 5. Where new parts are combined with used parts, only the cost of the new parts qualifies. You cannot claim both full expensing and the 50% first-year allowance against the same expenditure.
scope.from_when: Expenditure incurred on or after 1 April 2023
scope.how_to_claim: Must be claimed on the Company Tax Return. HMRC also provides an eligibility checker tool on the full expensing guidance page.

notes: Companies only — this is the single most-misstated point in third-party content, and HMRC's wording is unambiguous. The asset must be new and unused: second-hand kit goes to the Annual Investment Allowance or writing-down allowances instead. gov.uk's live guidance states the qualifying window as 'bought from 1 April 2023' with no end date, consistent with full expensing having been made permanent. Two further manual points worth knowing: second-hand components broken down and reformed into a new asset are treated as unused and not second-hand, and computer software is plant but for companies falls within the intangible fixed assets regime unless they elect out. HMRC's manual lists the general exclusions by reference to CAA 2001 s.46(2) and the page read here sets out only exclusions 2, 5 and 6, so no claim is made here about cessation-period expenditure, gifts or connected persons.

scope.who: Anyone who pays HMRC late is charged late payment interest; anyone owed money by HMRC may receive repayment interest. The main rates cover Income Tax, National Insurance contributions, Capital Gains Tax, Stamp Duty Land Tax, Stamp Duty, Stamp Duty Reserve Tax, VAT (for periods starting on or after 1 January 2023), Alcohol Duty (from 1 September 2025) and Vaping Product Duty (from 1 October 2026).
scope.excluded: Corporation Tax paid by quarterly instalments is not charged the main rates — separate and lower rates apply under 'Other Corporation Tax Self Assessment interest rates': 6.50% on underpaid instalments and 3.75% on overpaid instalments and on early payments of Corporation Tax not due by instalments, both from 16 November 2026. Taxpayers who pay in full and on time are charged no late payment interest at all. Repayment interest is not paid at the main rate below its 0.5% floor, which caps how far it can fall.
scope.from_when: 9 January 2026 for the 7.75% and 2.75% rates currently in force; 24 November 2026 for the 8.00% and 3.00% rates
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. Interest is applied automatically by HMRC — charged on amounts paid late, and added to repayments where due.

notes: Timing matters here and is easy to get wrong: as at 14 November 2026 the rates in force are 7.75% late payment and 2.75% repayment, set from 9 January 2026. The Bank Rate rise to 4% on 5 November 2026 feeds through to HMRC's rates on 24 November 2026, when they become 8.00% and 3.00%. Any copy published now should either state the current rates with the 24 November change flagged, or be dated. Late payment interest is not a penalty — it runs in addition to any late payment penalties. The next Bank Rate decision is 17 December 2026, so this subject can move again before the end of the year.

scope.who: People with gaps in their National Insurance record who do not have enough qualifying years for the full new State Pension and are not eligible for National Insurance credits. Class 3 is paid at £18.40 a week; some self-employed people can pay Class 2 at £3.65 a week instead. You can pay only for gaps in the past 6 tax years, with each deadline falling on 5 April — the deadline for a 2025 to 2026 gap is 5 April 2032. People below State Pension age can ask the Future Pension Centre whether paying will benefit them.
scope.excluded: You cannot pay if you have no gaps in your record, unless you are getting Class 3 credits and are eligible to pay Class 2 contributions. Married women and widows paying reduced rate National Insurance cannot pay voluntary contributions. You cannot pay once the deadline for the period with the gap has passed, so gaps older than 6 tax years are closed. People already eligible for National Insurance credits may not need to pay, and people who have reached State Pension age should contact the Pension Service (or, if abroad or recently abroad, the International Pension Centre) first because paying may not help.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 for the £18.40 weekly rate
scope.how_to_claim: You must check your National Insurance record and State Pension forecast, confirm that paying will benefit you, and then pay. HMRC updates the record after payment — up to 5 working days through the State Pension forecast service, or up to 8 weeks by other payment methods. People who have lived or worked abroad must check what to do before paying, as a different route applies.

notes: Two warnings that belong in any copy on this. First, paying does not always help: gov.uk states plainly that 'voluntary contributions do not always increase your State Pension', for example where you were contracted out — so the forecast check comes before the payment, not after. Second, Class 2 at £3.65 a week is far cheaper than Class 3 at £18.40, so eligibility for Class 2 should be checked first. The normal limit is the past 6 tax years with a 5 April deadline; gov.uk gives 5 April 2032 for a 2025/26 gap, and no extended deadline is currently advertised. Deadline dates for individual earlier years beyond that one example were not stated at primary source, so only the 6-year rule and the 2025/26 date are reported here rather than a derived year-by-year table.
